Danish freight intermediary Scan Global Logistics has made the largest investment in its history, agreeing to acquire Portland, Oregon-based logistics provider OIA Global in a deal it said late Wednesday that would put the company among the top 20 freight forwarders in the world.
Scan Global Logistics said the proposed acquisition will strengthen its presence in key markets and expand supply chain capabilities available to customers beyond traditional freight forwarding.
Founded in 1988, OIA Global employs more than 1,200 people across more than 60 offices in over 30 countries. Its capabilities span freight forwarding, customs brokerage, contract logistics, project logistics, prime contractor management, packaging design and materials management. OIA had $780 million in revenue last year.
Scan said the acquisition will complement its existing offering while significantly strengthening its position in the United States and other strategically important markets. The combination will also provide customers access to a broader range of supply chain solutions, making it easier to manage increasingly complex supply chains.
Why It Matters: Acquisitions, mergers and investments in the logistics industry have accelerated this year, especially in the United States, as the freight cycle turns more positive.
Armstrong & Associates ranks Scan as the 19th largest freight forwarder in the world based on gross revenue and ocean/air volume. It is near the top 50 logistics providers by gross revenue. Full-scale logistics providers provide warehousing, distribution and supply chain management in addition to arranging freight transportation for cargo owners.
Scan has rapidly expanded since 2018 through a series of acquisitions in Africa, Europe, and North America, and has also opened offices in several other countries. In 2021, it bought the international forwarding division of U.S. trucking giant Werner Enterprises . Scan has more than 5,100 employees and operates more than 200 offices around the world.
The company had $2.82 billion in revenue last year. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was up 12% year over year to $244.2 million. Scan lost $101.5 million, which management attributed to refinancing of debt and financing the acquisition of ITN Logistics Group in Canada.
The OIA transaction is subject to customary regulatory approvals. Terms of the deal, which is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, were not disclosed.

source_document.body:
BYD dealership in Thailand (Source: BYD)
BYD now has more than 1.02 million employees, according to chairman Wang Chuanfu. That’s more people than Toyota, GM, Ford, and Tesla employ combined.
And it’s a big jump from the start of the year. BYD reported about 869,600 employees at the end of 2025, which means the Chinese automaker has added roughly 150,000 people in 10 months while its vehicle sales are down.
Roughly 960,000 of BYD’s people work in China and about 60,000 work abroad. Up to 120,000 of them are R&D engineers, according to Wang, who shared the figures on stage Wednesday at the China Society of Automotive Engineers’ (CSAE) 33rd annual conference. Their work covers battery cells, motors, electronic controls, and semiconductors.
Wang credits vertical integration for that scale. In his telling, keeping batteries, chips, and motors in-house is what took BYD from a battery maker founded in 1994 to the world’s top-selling new energy vehicle brand several years running. He called the company’s rise a microcosm of China’s auto industry going from follower to leader.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
BYD’s headcount keeps swinging
BYD’s workforce has been all over the place in the last few years.
The company had about 570,100 employees at the end of 2022 and 703,500 at the end of 2023. Then it went on a hiring spree. We reported in September 2024 that BYD had passed 900,000 employees and claimed the largest R&D workforce of any automaker, with over 110,000 engineers. It ended 2024 with 968,900 people.
Then came the first big cut. BYD’s 2025 annual report showed roughly 869,600 employees at year-end, a drop of about 99,000, mostly in frontline production jobs.
Now it’s back over a million. Data compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence put BYD at 911,900 employees at the end of June, so the company added more than 100,000 people in about four months.
How BYD compares to other automakers
The gap with legacy automakers is massive. Volkswagen Group, which counts its Chinese joint ventures, reported 662,942 employees at the end of 2025. Toyota had 390,927 as of March 31, 2026, and Stellantis had 258,668 at the end of last year.
In the US, Ford ended 2025 with 169,000 employees and GM with 156,000. Tesla reported a worldwide headcount of 134,785 in its latest 10-K.
Add up Toyota, GM, Ford, and Tesla and you get about 851,000 people. BYD has roughly 170,000 more than that.
But headcount isn’t output. If you divide 2025 global vehicle sales by year-end workforce, BYD comes out far behind:
BYD sold about 4.6 million vehicles last year with 869,600 employees, or 5.3 vehicles per worker. Tesla delivered 1,636,129 vehicles with 134,785 people, about 12 per worker, and Volkswagen Group was at about 13.5. Toyota, with 11.3 million group sales including Daihatsu and Hino, got roughly 29 vehicles out of each employee.
There’s a catch, and it’s a big one. BYD’s headcount isn’t only a car company’s headcount. It includes BYD Electronic, its majority-owned contract manufacturer that assembles devices for other brands and reported 165,000 employees of its own at the end of 2025. It also covers BYD’s battery business, which supplies other automakers, plus its in-house chips, motors, energy storage, and rail transit operations.
In short, BYD’s vertical integration largely drives its high headcount.
Hiring while sales slip
BYD sold 3,131,576 vehicles in the first nine months of 2026, down 3.9% year-over-year. September was its best month of the year at 463,561 units, but the company has been stuck in a brutal price war at home and is losing ground to rivals like Geely and Leapmotor. Its first-half revenue (344.8 billion yuan) and net profit (12.3 billion yuan) were both down year-over-year.
All of the growth is overseas. BYD’s international sales hit 1,342,960 units through September, up 92.7%, and they now make up about 43% of its total volume. That’s on top of BYD beating Tesla on pure EV deliveries again in Q2 .
Yet only 60,000 of its 1.02 million workers are based outside China. That’s about 6%. So BYD is still building nearly everything at home and shipping it out, even as its factories in Thailand, Brazil, and Hungary come online.
Electrek’s Take
The 1.02 million number makes for a great headline, but we wouldn’t read it as a sign of strength on its own.
BYD’s whole model is to make almost everything itself: cells, chips, motors, seats, and a lot more. That’s a big reason it can sell a Seagull for around $10,000 in China and still make money. But it’s a labor-heavy model, and it works because Chinese factory labor is relatively cheap and plentiful. Toyota gets more than five times as many cars out of each employee. Tesla gets more than twice as many.
The problem is that BYD’s growth is now outside China, and that’s where this model gets tested. Only 6% of its workforce is abroad, yet 43% of its sales are. Tariffs in Europe, Brazil, Mexico, and elsewhere are pushing BYD to build locally, but a factory in Hungary or Brazil won’t necessarily produce the same.
The number that should worry legacy automakers is the 120,000 engineers. That’s almost as many people as Tesla employs in total, all working on product.

Forget about the 600+ hp hybrid-powered Polestar 1 supercoupe; the car that established Polestar as a standalone brand was the 2. As the brand pulls out of the US and shifts its focus to the rest of the world, it’s time to look back at the EV that helped define Polestar, along with a look around at some of the best EV deals of all time.
A number of European news sites (including Electrive and TV2 Broom ) are reporting that the last new Polestar 2 has rolled off the company’s Luqiao assembly line, with more than 200,000 of the all-electric sedan/hatchbacks built in China since the electric sedan launched in 2020. And, while the company hasn’t confirmed that with any sort of official announcement, the news jives with the company’s previously announced plans to release an updated Polestar 2 in 2027 , followed by an all-new Polestar 7 SUV that’s set to follow in early 2028.
With the brand set to pull out of the US after the Trump Administration’s Commerce Department declined to grant it authorization under the Connected Vehicle Rule earlier this year , it might at first seem like that US Polestar fans will miss out on that freshened 2, whatever shape it takes – but don’t lose hope, yet.
Volvo Concept 40.2
2016 Volvo Concept 40.2; by Volvo.
First shown in 2016, the original Volvo Concept 40.2 was supposed to be a new, entry-level sedan for the now Geely-owned Volvo , which was in the process of separating itself from Ford ownership and the Focus-based C30 coupe and S40/V50 sedan and wagons. And a fine entry-level Volvo it would have been, too, if Tesla’s share price hadn’t made it worth more than the next five most valuable car companies combined.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
See, once Tesla (or, more to the point, $TSLA) did that, every carmaker in the world figured the stock market would bless them with billions, too, and started announcing plans to go all electric, right now. Volvo parent company Geely, however, decided they’d fast-track the process, taking the next two Volvo models in their pipeline (the C90 coupe version of the S90 sedan and the C40 sedan previewed by the Concept 40.2) and made them Polestars.
A SPAC merger later, and Polestar was spun off as not only its own brand, but its own, largely Chinese-owned company – which brings us to where we are now.
The best EV deals in the business
Polestar 4. Photo: Polestar.
In the US the Polestar 3 Long-Range Single Motor (RWD) SUV starts at something like $67,500 and offers a 111 kWh battery pack good for an EPA-rated range of up to 350 miles. The top-shelf Performance-spec Polestar 3, meanwhile, offers an all-wheel-drive dual-motor setup that Polestar rates at 380 kW (~517 hp) that will launch you across suburbia with a 0–60 mph time in the 4 second range, albeit with slightly less range than the base model … but that $67,500 price is really more of a suggestion these days.
Polestar is offering a $23,000 discount on the 3 and a $25,000 , rebate, market adjustment or whatever on the 4. That means that you can get a brand new Polestar 3 or 4 with Chinese EV tech and more than a little bit of Volvo safety baked in for a dramatically reduced price. If you pick the right one at the right dealer, probably for less than $40,000.
As for the 2, I have a bit of a personal connection to that one. My son picked up a 19,000 mile 2024 Polestar 2 Long-Range Single Motor (RWD) in Glacier for under $22K, which is an absolutely shocking price for a fast, capable sporty sedan hatchback that isn’t just a worthy successor to the S40 it was meant to replace, but a solid foundation for an EV brand that got wrapped up in politics.

Boreas Is a Rugged Yet Refined Sprinter Camper Van Built for Four-Season Adventures
33 photos
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / White River Overland
Versatility is the name of the game when it comes to camper vans. In my opinion, a proper build will be able to tackle a wide range of scenarios, keeping you comfortable regardless of how you adventure. That's exactly what this camper van can do – meet Boreas.
Boreas is a conversion based on a 2024 AWD Mercedes-Benz Sprinter with a 144" wheelbase. It was created by White River Overland, an Aspen, Colorado-based company specializing in, as it shared, "designing and building semi-custom van conversions, overland vehicles, and truck upgrades engineered for four-season mountain travel."
White River Overland describes Boreas as the "ultimate Colorado rig." To it, that means it can handle things like day-to-day runs on asphalt, skiing adventures, backcountry driving, and more. As always, let's start the tour with the exterior.
The van rides on 17-inch bronze Reika Rambler wheels wrapped in Falken Wildpeak all-terrain tires. To improve the off-road capabilities, the builders installed a Van Compass Stage 4.3 suspension kit, which comes with front and rear Falcon adjustable shocks.
At the back, you'll find a heavy-duty swing-away bike rack and an Owl Vans spare tire carrier/ladder combo. Use it to climb on top of the vehicle and you'll discover a flat-mounted Starlink antenna, a 10-foot Thule awning, and a 225 W solar array. The company also made two cut-outs for a Maxxair vent fan and a Nomadic Cooling A/C unit.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / White River Overland Other notable mods are Owl Vans steps, Rigid scene lights on the sides, an Arctic Tern awning-style window, and flares. Flares, also known as pods or capsules, are designed to increase the van width to allow you to install a bed inside in an east to west arrangement instead of the standard north to south.
This rig's Vanspeed capsules are color matched to the van's body and come with half-slider windows.
Pull on the sliding door's handle, and it will open by itself. Enter, and a well-thought-out interior will greet you. One of the first things you'll notice is the open layout, with no wall separating the driver's cabin from the living space.
The driver and passenger seats are mounted on factory swivel bases, so they can be turned around to face the back of the van. What's more, White River Overland added a Wolfbox Pro G9000 dash cam/digital mirror, as well as a Van Wife Components headliner shelf.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / White River Overland Regarding aesthetics, the customer opted for grey laminated ply cabinetry, grey 2tec2 woven vinyl flooring, and slatted wall panels with a black background.
Straight ahead of the entrance, you'll come across a small bench, which can be described as the continuation of the front seating area. Between the bench and the driver's seat, you'll find a Lagun table mount with a folding top that can be adjusted to be reached from wherever you sit.
The bench integrates a decently sized drawer with a magnetic closure system. Above, you'll find a cabinet next to a touchscreen display for monitoring and controlling the power system.
Next, we have a kitchen, which is split into two units. The one on the passenger side features a deep black stainless steel sink with a retractable faucet, a drawer, and two lower cabinets. On the side of the counter, the builders added a panel with switches for four different lights, as well as one for a water pump.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / White River Overland One of the cabinets hides a Laveo dry-flush toilet on a slide-out. The slide-out is heavy-duty, so it can support the weight of a human – that means you can sit straight down and do your business without having to first remove the toilet.
The unit on the opposite side is meant mostly for storage. It has a fridge with a tiny freezer compartment, a tambour door hiding a pantry, a RecPro microwave oven, and a floor-to-ceiling closet with hanging space.
The rear part of the living space is taken up by, like in most vans, the bedroom. The customer chose a space-maximizing setup with a Murphy bed and abundant storage space.
On the driver's side, White River Overland added the Murphy bed platform, which, during the day or when you don't need the bed, is secured upright.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / White River Overland Setting up the bed is quick and easy – lower the platform, which rests on a unit on the other side, and then unfold a custom mattress made up of multiple pieces. To climb on it, you can use a slide-out step.
The bed platform sits on top of a unit that, besides offering some room to store your items, also accommodates a 48V power system.
Its highlights are a 7.2 kWh capacity and a 3,000 W inverter. Three charging sources are available: solar power, shore power, and DC-DC charging while the engine is running.
As for plumbing, the van is equipped with a 30-gallon (113-liter) freshwater tank, an under-mounted greywater tank, an electric water heater, and an outdoor shower connection.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / White River Overland This part of the van also has four overhead cabinets, a smart TV attached to a swivel mount, and a Maxxair vent fan above.
There's one more important amenity in this rig, one that hides in plain sight: a shower. By the entrance, you can lift a floor mat and reveal a teak shower mat sitting on top of a stainless steel pan. To complete the shower setup, you need to hang a curtain to the ceiling and connect a showerhead to the sink faucet.
All in all, Boreas by White River Overland pairs luxury with ruggedness in an aesthetically pleasing design suitable for a vast range of uses. What's really impressive is the number of comforts it manages to fit despite being built on a short wheelbase Sprinter van.

By Fleet Hero
29 October 2026
There is a moment every flatbed driver knows well. You are standing in the yard, coffee in hand, looking at a load that needs to move by morning. All the necessary American truck parts are packed: the tarp is folded on the catwalk, and the straps are coiled and ready. Everything looks fine. Then you realize you never actually measured the load. You guessed. And that guess is about to cost you money, time, or both.
It happens every single day across the country. Drivers skip the tape because they have hauled similar loads before. They assume the height is close enough. They figure the width will be fine. That assumption travels with them onto the highway, and it does not end well.
Use American Truck Parts Properly: The Tarp Will Tell You the Truth Eventually
The tarp isn’t some soft blanket that allows for mistakes in measuring. The tarp is cut to exact specifications. Should you lay the tarp over cargo which is taller than you anticipated, the tarp will pull tight on the edges, while the center drops down. Wind gets inside that loose fabric almost right away. At sixty-five miles per hour, that tarp flapping against the trailer becomes something which will batter the stitching of the tarp itself.
Straps Lose Their Grip When Angles Change
Every strap in American truck parts has a working load limit. That limit assumes a specific angle between the strap and the cargo. When the load is taller or wider than planned, that angle changes. A strap that should run at forty-five degrees might end up nearly vertical. Vertical straps lose holding power. Tension concentrates on one point instead of spreading across the load. Webbing stretches. Hardware bends. The cargo shifts.
Corner protectors are supposed to prevent this by creating a smooth surface for the strap to slide across. But if the dimensions are wrong, the protectors sit in the wrong place. The strap rubs directly against rough cargo. Friction eats through the webbing. A strap that should last years fails in one trip.
Permits Are Legal Documents, Not Suggestions
Oversize and overweight permits list exact dimensions of American truck parts. If you apply for a permit with a height of fourteen feet, that permit covers a load measuring fourteen feet. Not fourteen feet six inches. Not fifteen feet. The number on the paper has to match the number on the road.
Bridge strikes in New York reached 350 in 2024, according to the governor’s office , which is why its “Check Your Height” campaign is now running in 16 states and Washington, D.C., and why it warns that consumer-grade GPS can steer trucks onto low-clearance routes. A navigation app cannot know how tall a tarped load really is, so the measurement has to come from a tape, not a screen.
That warning applies everywhere.
Building Better Habits Behind the Wheel
Measure height with the tarp installed. Measure width at the widest point, including overhang. Measure length for the full combination. Scale the load and record axle weights. Write everything down. Recheck after any adjustment.
These steps take five minutes. A bridge strike takes hours. A rejected permit takes days. A load that shifts because the straps were never going to hold takes lives.
Measurement is not glamorous work. Nobody brags about measuring a load correctly. But it is the work that keeps tarps intact, straps tight, and permits valid. Drivers who treat measurement as a core part of the job spend less time fixing problems on the shoulder and more time delivering loads the way they were planned.
This article was sponsored by Fleet Hero.

They day you get to book an all-electric flight may be closer than you think if Dutch startup Elysian Aircraft gets its way. Their new E9X commercial airliner promises flights that are a whole lot quieter, and at prices that are whole lot less dependent on dumb oil wars .
Aircraft account for more than 2% of global heating when CO₂ and other emissions are taken into account, with the share considerably higher in wealthy countries, according to data cited by climate campaign group Stay Grounded . Elysian Aircraft is keenly aware of the industry’s climate impact, and they believe their planned full-size electric airliner will be perfectly positioned to make a dramatic difference.
“By being able to transport 90 passengers for initially 800 kilometers and eventually 1,000 kilometers you can reduce emissions to zero, from half the world’s flights,” Elysian co-founder Daniel Jacobson told EuroNews . “That is a very large amount of flight activity in the world. And you reduce total emissions from aerospace by 20%.”
The thing, itself
E9X electric aircraft; via Elysian.
At the core of those ambitious emission-reduction goals is the Elysian E9X aircraft. Designed in collaboration with aerospace researchers at Delft University of Technology (TU Delft), the E9X packs its oversized wings with modular battery packs, sending power to six propellers driven by electric motors.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Specs on those haven’t been revealed, but the E9X is designed to carry up to 100 passengers up to 1,000 km (~620 miles) from where they started. Elysian says that’s enough range to handle nearly 50% of scheduled commercial passenger flights worldwide and potentially eliminate 20% of total in-flight emissions when the plane enters service in 2034.
That said, the E9X is far more than “just a concept,” and Elysian has completed its second conceptual design review and flown a scaled demonstrator in concert with Germany’s DLR aerospace research center , demonstrating how its unique battery packaging solutions address the challenges of integrating heavy battery packs into an aircraft’s wings (where fuel is traditionally stored).
Top comment by D B
Liked by 1 people
A range of 620 miles at 400 mph cruise speed means approx 1.5 hours duration.
However the FAA generally mandates a 45-minute fuel reserve for domestic flights, while EASA and ICAO standards require a 30-minute reserve. This is to accommodate delays in landing, a missed approach, or to deviate to an alternate destination. Typically there is also a contingency reserve to account for unforeseen events like route deviations or headwinds.
Taking that into account, what will the true range be?
View all comments
The company is also working with airline partners KLM and Transavia to explore the operational and commercial requirements for putting electric airliners into service, with aircraft lessor TrueNoord investigating how the E9X could be financed and supported commercially.

source_document.body:
2026 SEMA Show • Mitsubishi Returns to Las Vegas With the Fresh 2028 Outlander Diamond Trail Edition
20-Year-Old Drives His Dad's 1968 Ford Galaxie, He's Been Working on It Since He Was Eight
19 photos
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube
While most young people want the latest, fastest, most technologically advanced cars of their time, this young man drives a Ford Galaxie from when his parents were younger than he is today. He has been dreaming of driving the 1968 fastback since he was eight. He is doing it now, getting a gazillion thumbs-ups and smiles wherever he goes.
Morgan is 20 years old and drives a 1968 Ford Galaxie that rolled off the production line when his parents were kids in school. His father bought the car 18 years ago. It became his 12 years ago, when he was just eight.
His father wasn't interested in the car much, but young Morgan was. He has been working on it since, dreaming of driving it one day, while kids his age were just learning to tie their shoelaces. He has always loved old cars because they are easy to work on and they get thumbs-ups and smiles wherever they go. His 1968 Galaxie is spotlight-guaranteed.
Rust has bitten big chunks of the body, which was repainted in the original colors in the early 1990s, but Morgan doesn’t really mind. It’s patina, and he is a fan of naturally created patina. He's going to lay a clear coat on top of it to preserve it.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube However, he can only imagine how his car looked when it rolled off the production line back in 1968. The interior isn’t doing any better either. The original seats are split open. That is exactly why he covered them up in colorful fabric. The car rides on aftermarket American Racing wheels, supposedly from the late 1980s or early 1990s.
He doesn't make plans when it comes to his good, old Galaxie. He is well aware that it might give in and leave him stranded any day. However, he will know how to fix it. Morgan just wants to keep it on the road for as long as he can and enjoy it.
In the meantime, he hopes to convince young people his age to buy classic American steel. And it is working! His friend Walter has recently bought a 1958 Oldsmobile Super 88, a model released during GM’s Golden Anniversary year that was widely known back in the day as “The King of Chrome.”
When new, a 1968 Ford Galaxie like his own carried an MSRP ranging from $2,860 to $3,320, depending on the trim level and body style. Adjusted for inflation to today’s money, that original buying power translates to approximately $26,200 to $30,400.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube Today, the value of a nearly 60-year-old Galaxie depends on condition, powertrain configuration, and, of course, body style. Project cars sit anywhere between $1,500 and $8,000, according to Hagerty, but they might not exactly be cars that run and drive.
Meanwhile, highly original low-mileage survivors or professionally restored models regularly command prices between $15,000 and $28,000. Then, there are the concours, rare fastbacks and pristine convertibles, which can fetch up to $50,000.
Morgan road-tripped his Ford 1,000 miles over the weekend with zero issues, which is quite impressive for a car this age. That’s more than this car has traveled in the past years combined. For most of the time, it either sat or averaged just 25 miles per year.
His Galaxie is powered by the 302-cubic-inch (5.0-liter) Challenger V8 engine under the hood, paired with a two-barrel carburetor. The V8 pushes out 210 horsepower (213 metric horsepower) and 295 pound-feet (400 Newton meters) of torque.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube Because the Galaxie was a massive, full-sized family car, measuring 213.3 inches (5,418 millimeters) in length and weighing roughly 3,820 pounds (1,733 kilograms) in fastback form , the small-block 302 engine provided steady cruising power rather than blistering muscle car speed. That is why it takes 11.3 long seconds to hit 60 mph (97 kph) from a standstill, on its way to a top speed of 111 mph (178 kph). It was far from a sports car, but it is spacious, reliable, and easy to maintain.
Morgan’s Galaxie is the XL trim , which was Ford's attempt at selling a car with a high-end package designed to give their full-sized flagship car a European-inspired grand touring flair. And it obviously worked. Debuting in 1962, the "XL" lettering referred to "Extra Lively," as the model tried to bridge the gap between heavy executive luxury and aggressive, big-block muscle car performance.
The trim brought all-vinyl front bucket seats, split down the middle by a bright chrome-trimmed center console, the iconic U-Grip automatic handle, or a manual stick shift mounted in the floor instead of the column shifter, and special door-mounted courtesy lights.
The Galaxie XL was also easy to recognize from outside. While standard models featured exposed dual horizontal headlights, the XL came with a unique, aggressively styled grille, featuring vacuum-operated hideaway headlights.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube To get it back on the road earlier this year, Morgan had to replace the fuel pump. His car wears the Mooneyes sticker. In car culture, placing a "MOON Equipped" decal on a vehicle meant it was outfitted with high-quality, American-made performance or styling parts built right in Moon's machine shop.
Founded by legendary hot rodder Dean Moon in 1950 as MOON Automotive in Santa Fe Springs, California, the brand is universally recognized by its famous "double eyeball" logo. Moon was a charter member of SEMA (Specialty Equipment Market Association) and famously let Carroll Shelby build the very first Shelby Cobra inside the Moon garage in 1962.
The 1968 Ford Galaxie is not the only means of transportation for Morgan. He also has a 1990 GMC 2500 truck at home. That is definitely his daily driver in winter. The Galaxie is for the rest of the year.
